title: Epidemiological foundations
objective: Define the population, outcome, denominator and time period before choosing an analysis.
summary: Define the population, selection process, outcome and time horizon first. Prevalence counts existing cases in a population at a specified time or period. Incidence concerns new cases: cumulative risk concerns initially disease-free people over a fixed period, whereas an incidence rate uses their time at risk. Changing diagnosis counts can reflect population size, testing or case definitions, not just disease occurrence. Study design and ascertainment determine what comparisons mean.
challenge: A clinic sees twice as many new diagnoses this year. Which population, testing and time-period information would you need before concluding that disease risk has doubled?
steps: This fictional one-year cohort starts with 300 disease-free exposed and 300 disease-free unexposed people, with complete follow-up and comparable case ascertainment. There are 30 and 15 first cases respectively. The risk form takes four cell counts, not group totals: columns are exposed/unexposed and rows are outcome present/absent. Enter top row 30, 15 and bottom row 270, 285. Then one-year risks are 10% and 5%, RR = 2 and exposed-minus-unexposed risk difference = 5 percentage points. These are observational associations; they do not by themselves establish an exposure effect.
r:
# Fictional cohort: initially disease-free people, complete one-year follow-up,
# comparable case ascertainment; events are first cases in distinct people.
events <- c(30,15); at_risk <- c(300,300)
print(data.frame(Group=c("Exposed","Unexposed"),Events=events,At_risk=at_risk,Risk=events/at_risk))
print(c(risk_ratio=(30/300)/(15/300),risk_difference=30/300-15/300))
barplot(events/at_risk,names.arg=c("Exposed","Unexposed"),ylim=c(0,0.15),ylab="One-year risk",main="Observed association, not a causal estimate")
# If follow-up durations differ, examine person-time and censoring; do not label these risks incidence rates.

title: From association to causal questions
objective: Recognise confounding and define the assumptions behind a causal comparison.
summary: A causal question compares well-defined alternatives in the same target population. Baseline age can influence exposure and outcome, making the exposed groups incomparable. Adjustment needs a justified causal structure and assumptions, not just a change in an estimate. Conditioning on a mediator can remove part of a total effect and does not automatically identify a direct effect; conditioning on a common consequence can induce selection bias.
challenge: Age can affect both treatment choice and outcome. Why might adjusting for age help, while adjusting for a consequence of treatment change the effect we are trying to estimate?
steps: Assume initially disease-free people, complete one-year follow-up and age measured before exposure. Constructed counts are 44/200 exposed versus 26/200 unexposed. For the crude risk grid, columns are exposed/unexposed and rows are outcome present/absent: enter top row 44, 26 and bottom row 156, 174. Younger risks are 4/40 and 16/160; older risks are 40/160 and 10/40. Crude RR is about 1.69, but each within-age RR is 1. Standardising both groups to a 50% younger, 50% older population gives risk 17.5% in each. This illustrates age imbalance; neither equality after adjustment nor a crude association proves a causal conclusion.
r:
# Constructed baseline-age example: initially disease-free people,
# first cases over one year with complete follow-up. Age precedes exposure.
data <- data.frame(Age=c("Younger","Older"),Exposed_events=c(4,40),Exposed_total=c(40,160),Unexposed_events=c(16,10),Unexposed_total=c(160,40))
data$Exposed_risk <- data$Exposed_events/data$Exposed_total
data$Unexposed_risk <- data$Unexposed_events/data$Unexposed_total
print(data)
print(c(crude_RR=(44/200)/(26/200)))
print(data.frame(Age=data$Age,Within_age_RR=data$Exposed_risk/data$Unexposed_risk))
# Apply the SAME target-population weights to both groups.
weights <- c(0.5,0.5)
standardised <- c(Exposed=sum(weights*data$Exposed_risk),Unexposed=sum(weights*data$Unexposed_risk))
print(standardised)
print(c(standardised_RR=unname(standardised[1]/standardised[2])))
barplot(rbind(data$Exposed_risk,data$Unexposed_risk),beside=TRUE,names.arg=data$Age,legend.text=c("Exposed","Unexposed"),ylab="Observed risk",main="Same within-age risks; different age mix")
# Within-stratum agreement is not proof that every source of bias has been removed.

title: Comparing paired measurements
objective: Recognise pairing, analyse differences and interpret a confidence interval.
summary: Pairing means repeated measurements on the same people or explicitly matched units. A paired t test analyses within-pair differences, with independence between pairs. For exact small-sample inference the differences are normally distributed; inspect their distribution and unusual values. Two sets of patients attending the same clinic at different times are not automatically paired, and different patients may still be clustered.
challenge: The example has a before and an after measurement on each of the same eight people. Why is a paired analysis appropriate, and what design questions would you ask if the two periods instead contained different, unmatched people?
steps: Use Try in StatsDirect to open the paired t test with Before and After. The worksheet contains eight fictional, independently sampled participants. The comparison is Before minus After, so a positive difference means a fall. Use a 95% confidence level to compare with the R example. Inspect the differences and interpret the estimated mean difference and interval before the P value; an uncontrolled before–after change alone does not establish causation.
r:
# Fictional paired measurements: same eight people, same row order.
before <- c(142,136,151,145,139,148,132,155)
after <- c(135,134,143,141,136,140,130,147)
data <- data.frame(Before=before, After=after)
print(data)
# StatsDirect uses first minus second for this selection.
# Assume independent people; small-sample t inference models normal differences.
change <- before - after
print(t.test(before, after, paired=TRUE, conf.level=0.95))
plot(before, after, pch=19, xlab="Before", ylab="After", main="Fictional paired measurements")
abline(0,1,lty=2)
# The diagonal shows equal before/after values; this is not an agreement analysis.
# Try: inspect change, change one after value, rerun, and explain the interval.
# A change without a suitable control comparison does not establish causation.
previousChallenges: If the average measurement falls after an intervention, what else would you need before claiming the intervention caused the change?

title: Variation, precision and uncertainty
objective: Separate standard deviation from standard error and confidence intervals.
summary: Standard deviation describes variation between observations. Standard error describes sampling variation of an estimator. For independent observations from the same population, the mean has SE = population SD / sqrt(n), estimated using the sample SD. A nominal 95% confidence procedure targets 95% repeated-sampling coverage under its assumptions. These 12 waits are skewed: a small-sample t interval is an illustration to scrutinise, not an assurance of reliable coverage.
challenge: For independent observations from the same population with a fixed, finite variance, why does quadrupling sample size halve the theoretical standard error of the mean? Why might the sample SD and estimated SE still vary between samples?
steps: Open the descriptive summary for the fictional waiting times. Compare mean, median, SD and the 95% confidence interval. Inspect the long wait and the distribution before interpreting the small-sample t interval. Do not delete an observation merely because it is large. The appropriate summary depends on whether the question concerns an average, a typical wait or the long-wait tail. For these 12 values, StatsDirect and R t.test() both use a Student t interval for the mean with 11 degrees of freedom: approximately 13.8 to 24.8 minutes. Agreement between programs checks the calculation, not whether the model assumptions fit these skewed data.
r:
# Fictional clinic waits; no patient data.
wait <- c(12,15,14,18,21,16,19,13,45,17,20,22)
print(data.frame(Waiting_minutes=wait))
print(c(mean=mean(wait), median=median(wait), SD=sd(wait), SE=sd(wait)/sqrt(length(wait))))
# An illustrative Student t mean CI with 11 df, as in StatsDirect: only 12 skewed observations.
# Exact t coverage assumes independent normal observations; that is questionable here.
# A non-significant normality test would not establish the assumption.
mean_ci <- t.test(wait, conf.level=0.95)$conf.int
cat("Illustrative 95% t interval for the mean; check assumptions:\n")
print(mean_ci)
# Describe this as about 13.8 to 24.8 minutes; keep full values for calculations.
# Extra displayed decimals do not make the assumptions more credible.
hist(wait, breaks=8, main="Fictional clinic waiting times", xlab="Minutes")
# Try: explain why mean and median differ; inspect the outlier without silently deleting it.

title: Interpreting a diagnostic test
objective: Choose the right denominator for sensitivity, specificity and predictive value.
summary: Sensitivity is the proportion positive among people with the condition; specificity is the proportion negative among those without it. Predictive values condition on the test result instead. The fictional sample represents a population with 10% prevalence and a reliable reference diagnosis. Predictive values depend on prevalence; sensitivity and specificity also need to be applicable to the intended case mix, threshold and reference standard.
challenge: If the condition becomes rarer while sensitivity and specificity stay the same, what happens to the proportion of positive results that are false positives?
steps: In the diagnostic grid, columns represent disease present/absent and rows test positive/negative: enter top row 72, 81 and bottom row 18, 729. These are true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives respectively. These fictional independent observations give sensitivity 80%, specificity 90%, PPV about 47.1% and NPV about 97.6%. For sensitivity, StatsDirect and R binom.test() both use the Clopper–Pearson exact binomial method: the 95% interval is about 70.2% to 87.7%. This interval concerns sensitivity, not PPV; matching inputs, confidence level and method should give matching limits apart from rounding.
r:
# Fictional diagnostic study. Rows: test result; columns: disease status.
tp <- 72; fn <- 18; fp <- 81; tn <- 729
counts <- matrix(c(tp,fp,fn,tn),nrow=2,byrow=TRUE,dimnames=list(Test=c("Positive","Negative"),Disease=c("Present","Absent")))
print(counts)
print(c(sensitivity=tp/(tp+fn), specificity=tn/(tn+fp), PPV=tp/(tp+fp), NPV=tn/(tn+fn)))
# Treat diagnoses as reliable and observations as independent.
# StatsDirect and binom.test use the same Clopper-Pearson exact binomial method.
# This is a sensitivity interval, not an interval for all four measures.
sensitivity_ci <- binom.test(tp,tp+fn,conf.level=0.95)$conf.int
cat("95% Clopper-Pearson exact CI for sensitivity (may be conservative):\n")
print(sensitivity_ci)
barplot(counts, beside=TRUE, legend.text=TRUE, main="Fictional diagnostic counts", ylab="People")

misconceptions.correction: The intended population may have a different spectrum of disease and alternative diagnoses.

title: Absolute and relative benefit
objective: Interpret absolute risk reduction, relative risk and the follow-up period.
summary: Over one year, 28/200 controls and 16/200 programme participants have at least one unplanned admission. The estimated absolute risk reduction (control minus programme) is 6 percentage points; programme-to-control RR is about 0.57 and NNT for benefit rounds up to 17. These are uncertain point estimates. The illustrated risk-difference interval includes zero and possible harm, so it does not establish benefit. This example was chosen to lie near the conventional 5% significance boundary: interpret the effect size and uncertainty, and do not choose a method just to obtain significance.
challenge: Would the same relative risk imply the same absolute benefit in a population with a much lower baseline risk?
steps: Assume individual randomisation, independent participants and complete one-year follow-up. In the NNT form enter 16 people with at least one admission among 200 programme participants and 28 among 200 controls. Count people, not repeated admissions. Interpret NNT 17 as the point estimate for preventing one additional person having an admission over one year. A risk-difference interval spanning zero gives NNT uncertainty extending through infinity into both benefit and harm; do not present a single ordinary finite NNT interval. The R script explicitly computes the same Miettinen–Nurminen score interval as StatsDirect, including its finite-sample variance correction; it does not use the simpler Wald interval from two-sample prop.test().
r:
# Fictional individually randomised programme; complete one-year follow-up.
# Events count people with at least one admission, not repeated admissions.
events <- c(16,28); totals <- c(200,200)
risk <- events/totals
print(data.frame(Group=c("Programme","Usual care"),Events=events,Total=totals,Risk=risk))
arr <- risk[2]-risk[1]
print(c(absolute_reduction=arr,relative_risk=risk[1]/risk[2],NNT=if(arr==0) Inf else ceiling(1/abs(arr))))
cat("NNT point-estimate direction:",if(arr>0) "benefit" else if(arr<0) "harm" else "no difference", "\n")

# Explicit Miettinen-Nurminen score interval, as used by StatsDirect.
# This base-R helper inverts the constrained-binomial score with the N/(N-1)
# variance correction. It also handles zero-event and all-event groups.
# Its direction is the first risk minus the second. No extra R package is needed.
mn_interval <- function(x1,n1,x0,n0,conf.level=0.95) {
  args <- c(x1,n1,x0,n0,conf.level)
  stopifnot(all(lengths(list(x1,n1,x0,n0,conf.level))==1), all(is.finite(args)),
            n1>=1,n0>=1,x1>=0,x1<=n1,x0>=0,x0<=n0,
            all(args[1:4]==floor(args[1:4])), conf.level>0,conf.level<1)
  estimate <- x1/n1-x0/n0
  critical <- qchisq(conf.level,df=1)
  score <- function(d) {
    lo <- max(0,-d); hi <- min(1,1-d)
    derivative <- function(p0) {
      term <- function(x,n,p) {
        (if(x==0) 0 else x/p) - (if(x==n) 0 else (n-x)/(1-p))
      }
      term(x1,n1,p0+d)+term(x0,n0,p0)
    }
    if(lo==hi) p0 <- lo else {
      rises <- (lo+d<=0 && x1>0) || (lo<=0 && x0>0) || derivative(lo)>0
      falls <- (hi+d>=1 && x1<n1) || (hi>=1 && x0<n0) || derivative(hi)<0
      p0 <- if(!rises) lo else if(!falls) hi else
        uniroot(derivative,c(lo,hi),tol=1e-14,check.conv=TRUE)$root
    }
    p1 <- min(1,max(0,p0+d))
    variance <- (p1*(1-p1)/n1+p0*(1-p0)/n0)*(n1+n0)/(n1+n0-1)
    if(variance<=0) return(if(estimate==d) -critical else Inf)
    (estimate-d)^2/variance-critical
  }
  limits <- c(lower=if(estimate<= -1) -1 else uniroot(score,c(-1,estimate),tol=1e-13,check.conv=TRUE)$root,
              upper=if(estimate>= 1) 1 else uniroot(score,c(estimate,1),tol=1e-13,check.conv=TRUE)$root)
  attr(limits,"conf.level") <- conf.level
  limits
}
# Keep the interval direction consistent with arr: usual care minus programme.
arr_ci <- mn_interval(events[2],totals[2],events[1],totals[1])
cat("95% Miettinen-Nurminen interval for risk reduction, usual care minus programme:\n")
print(arr_ci,digits=10)

# Recalculate when changing the counts; these reference limits are not new data.
# This deliberately borderline example includes zero and possible harm.
# Do not change the method to seek a smaller P value. No single method is best
# for every design: these are independent binary outcomes, not paired/clustered data.
# Inverting an interval across zero needs separate benefit/harm branches via infinity.
# Do not report its reciprocals as one ordinary finite NNT interval.
barplot(risk,names.arg=c("Programme","Usual care"),ylim=c(0,0.2),ylab="One-year event risk")

keyConcepts.explanation: For this adverse outcome, control risk minus programme risk is the absolute risk reduction. Six percentage points is a difference of 0.06, not a 6% relative reduction.
An identical relative risk can imply different absolute differences in populations with different baseline risks, provided the relative effect is applicable.
NNT is a reciprocal of an absolute risk difference at a stated time horizon. If the difference interval crosses zero, its reciprocal has separate benefit and harm branches through infinity.

misconceptions.correction: The interval for the underlying risk difference includes no effect and possible harm.

misconceptions.claim: NNT counts admissions prevented, including repeated admissions in the same person.

For these counts, StatsDirect and the R script both give a Miettinen–Nurminen 95% interval of about −0.14 to 12.35 percentage points (−0.001445 to 0.123548 on the proportion scale). title: Association is not causation
objective: Interpret a regression slope without confusing prediction with causation.
summary: Each row is a different fictional service, with appointment duration and a mean satisfaction score on a 0–100 scale. The line describes a service-level association; it does not establish an individual-level or causal effect. Conventional small-sample regression inference assumes a linear conditional mean, independent errors with constant variance and normal errors. Inspect residuals and study design; the predictor need not be normally distributed.
challenge: A service with longer appointment slots has higher satisfaction. What alternative explanations could produce this association?
steps: Use Satisfaction as the dependent variable and Appointment minutes as the predictor in simple linear regression. The eight services are treated as independent for this illustration. Inspect the scatterplot and residuals; consider service case mix and measurement. The R intervals are 95% intervals for model coefficients, not prediction intervals for a future service. Do not extrapolate beyond 10–24 minutes without justification.
r:
# Eight fictional services: each row is a separate service, not a patient.
# Satisfaction is the service mean on a 0-100 scale.
# For conventional small-sample inference assume linear mean, independent,
# constant-variance normal errors. Predictor normality is not required.
data <- data.frame(Satisfaction=c(58,61,60,67,65,73,71,78),Minutes=c(10,12,14,16,18,20,22,24))
print(data)
fit <- lm(Satisfaction ~ Minutes, data=data)
print(summary(fit))
cat("95% confidence intervals for regression coefficients (not predictions):\n")
print(confint(fit,level=0.95))
plot(data$Minutes,data$Satisfaction,pch=19,xlab="Appointment minutes",ylab="Satisfaction",main="Association in fictional service data")
abline(fit)
plot(fitted(fit),residuals(fit),pch=19,xlab="Fitted satisfaction",ylab="Residual",main="Check the model, not just the slope")
abline(h=0,lty=2)
# Explain a potential service-level confounder; do not infer individual causation.

title: Comparing population rates
objective: Explain a crude rate difference using age-specific rates and a common standard population.
summary: A rate divides events by time at risk. Different age structures can produce different crude rates even when age-specific rates are identical. Direct standardisation applies the same reference weights to each population. A standardised rate is a comparison measure; report its reference population, uncertainty and age-specific pattern.
challenge: Two areas have identical younger and older age-specific rates but different crude rates. How could this happen, and what would a fair age-standardised comparison require?
steps: The worksheet has two rows: younger, then older. For Area A select Events (40, 800), Person-years (20000, 80000), then Reference population (75000, 25000) in Direct standardization. Use default row labels and multiplier 100000. The crude rate is 840 per 100000 person-years; the directly standardised rate is 400. Area B has 160 and 200 events in 80000 and 20000 person-years: its crude rate is 360 but the same standardised rate is 400. R displays both areas. Compare point estimates with matching units; StatsDirect also supplies intervals.
r:
# Fictional independent event counts; rows are younger, older.
# Person-time is time actually at risk, not the number of people enrolled.
area_a <- data.frame(Events=c(40,800),Person_years=c(20000,80000))
area_b <- data.frame(Events=c(160,200),Person_years=c(80000,20000))
reference <- c(75000,25000); weights <- reference/sum(reference)
rate_a <- area_a$Events/area_a$Person_years
rate_b <- area_b$Events/area_b$Person_years
crude <- c(A=sum(area_a$Events)/sum(area_a$Person_years),B=sum(area_b$Events)/sum(area_b$Person_years))*100000
standardised <- c(A=sum(weights*rate_a),B=sum(weights*rate_b))*100000
print(data.frame(Age=c("Younger","Older"),A_per_100000=rate_a*100000,B_per_100000=rate_b*100000,Weight=weights))
print(rbind(Crude=crude,Standardised=standardised))
barplot(rbind(Crude=crude,Standardised=standardised),beside=TRUE,legend.text=TRUE,ylab="Events per 100000 person-years",main="Fictional areas, common age-specific rates")
# Point-estimate illustration. Do not give this weighted rate the CI for a single crude count.
# Equal standardised rates do not prove equality or remove all sources of bias.

title: Appraising a trial result
objective: Explain what a numerical trial result can and cannot establish.
summary: Read the research question, allocation, follow-up and outcome measurement before the P value. Risk of bias concerns a particular result; reporting completeness and a large sample do not guarantee validity. Missing outcomes can break the comparability intended by randomisation. Explain effect size, uncertainty and applicability separately.
challenge: A randomised trial reports outcomes for 80 of 100 programme participants and all 100 controls. Before accepting its claim of benefit, what would you ask about the 20 missing outcomes?
steps: Fictional one-year adverse outcomes are observed in 20/80 programme participants and 30/100 controls. Try in StatsDirect opens the risk comparison: columns programme/control, top row events 20, 30; bottom row observed non-events 60, 70. The observed-data RR is 5/6. This omits 20 programme participants. R shows how their unknown outcomes permit full-group programme risks from 20% to 40%, against 30% in controls. These bounds describe missing-outcome uncertainty, not a 95% confidence interval.
r:
# Fictional individually randomised trial, one-year binary adverse outcome.
randomised <- c(Programme=100,Control=100)
observed <- c(Programme=80,Control=100)
events <- c(Programme=20,Control=30)
missing <- randomised-observed
print(data.frame(Randomised=randomised,Observed=observed,Events=events,Missing=missing))
observed_rr <- (events[1]/observed[1])/(events[2]/observed[2]); print(observed_rr)
programme_bounds <- c(Lower=20/100,Upper=(20+20)/100)
control_risk <- 30/100
arr_bounds <- c(Lower=control_risk-programme_bounds[2],Upper=control_risk-programme_bounds[1])
print(programme_bounds); print(arr_bounds)
plot(c(1,1),programme_bounds,type="b",pch=19,xlim=c(0.5,1.5),ylim=c(0,0.5),xaxt="n",xlab="Programme: possible one-year risk",ylab="Risk",main="Missing-outcome bounds, not a confidence interval")
abline(h=control_risk,lty=2)
legend("topleft", "Control risk: 30%", lty=2, bty="n")
# Bounds assume all 20 unknown outcomes are either non-events or events.
# They do not include sampling uncertainty or assert that either extreme is plausible.

title: Understanding missing data
objective: Describe missingness and avoid treating a filled-in value as observed information.
summary: Document the amount, pattern and reasons for missingness before choosing an analysis. MCAR, MAR and MNAR describe assumptions about the missingness process. MAR allows dependence on observed information; it is not a synonym for a random-looking pattern. Replacing missing values with a mean does not restore information or valid uncertainty.
challenge: Six of eight people return a symptom score. How might the interpretation change if the two missing people felt much worse, rather than simply forgetting an appointment?
steps: Scores range from 0 to 40, with higher scores worse. The StatsDirect worksheet contains only the six observed scores: 20, 22, 18, 26, 24, 30. Its mean is 23.33 for responders, not necessarily all eight people. R retains two explicit NA positions and shows full-group mean bounds of 17.5 to 27.5 if each missing score can lie anywhere from 0 to 40. This is an illustration of assumptions, not a confidence interval or a recommended imputation method.
r:
# Fictional scores, allowable range 0–40; higher is worse.
score <- c(20,22,18,26,24,30,NA,NA)
print(data.frame(Person=seq_along(score),Score=score,Missing=is.na(score)))
observed_mean <- mean(score,na.rm=TRUE)
mean_bounds <- (sum(score,na.rm=TRUE)+sum(is.na(score))*c(0,40))/length(score)
print(c(Observed_mean=observed_mean,Missing=sum(is.na(score))))
print(mean_bounds)
filled <- replace(score,is.na(score),observed_mean)
print(c(Observed_SD=sd(score,na.rm=TRUE),Mean_filled_SD=sd(filled)))
barplot(c(Observed_mean=observed_mean,Lower_bound=mean_bounds[1],Upper_bound=mean_bounds[2]),ylim=c(0,40),ylab="Symptom score",main="Missing values: bounds are not confidence limits")
# Mean filling is shown as a pitfall: it understates uncertainty if treated as real data.
# No method can identify the missing outcomes from these observed values alone.

keyConcepts.explanation: MCAR means missingness does not depend on observed or unobserved values. Under MAR, after conditioning on observed information it does not additionally depend on the missing values. Under MNAR that dependence remains.

Observed data alone cannot generally distinguish MAR from MNAR. Use reasons for absence, auxiliary measurements and scientifically defensible sensitivity scenarios.

title: Checking prediction performance
objective: Assess predictions against outcomes not used to develop the model.
summary: A model can rank outcomes well yet predict systematically wrong values. Evaluate calibration and prediction error as well as association. Performance on the development data is usually optimistic. Internal validation must repeat the modelling process; evaluation in a new relevant setting addresses transportability. A tiny illustration cannot establish clinical usefulness.
challenge: If we add ten points to every predicted score, can its correlation with observed scores stay unchanged while its prediction error gets worse?
steps: The fictional predictions were fixed before these eight outcomes were observed. Select Observed score as outcome and Predicted score as predictor in simple regression to inspect calibration; a descriptive calibration line is not a newly validated prediction model. R compares the original predictions with the same predictions shifted upward by ten. Correlation is unchanged; RMSE rises from about 1.58 to 10.12 points. Compare with the identity line, not just the fitted slope.
r:
# Fictional independent evaluation sample. Predictions were fixed in advance.
predicted <- seq(10,80,by=10)
observed <- c(12,18,31,39,51,59,72,78)
shifted <- predicted+10
rmse <- function(p) sqrt(mean((observed-p)^2))
print(data.frame(Observed=observed,Predicted=predicted,Shifted=shifted))
metrics <- rbind(Original=c(Correlation=cor(observed,predicted),RMSE=rmse(predicted),Mean_error=mean(predicted-observed)),Shifted=c(Correlation=cor(observed,shifted),RMSE=rmse(shifted),Mean_error=mean(shifted-observed)))
print(metrics)
calibration <- lm(observed~predicted); print(coef(calibration))
plot(predicted,observed,pch=19,xlim=c(0,100),ylim=c(0,100),xlab="Predicted score",ylab="Observed score",main="Correlation does not establish calibration")
points(shifted,observed,pch=1,col="blue"); abline(0,1,lty=2)
legend("topleft",c("Original","Shifted +10","Ideal agreement"),pch=c(19,1,NA),lty=c(NA,NA,2),col=c("black","blue","black"))
# This eight-person example demonstrates metrics; it does not validate clinical use.
# Do not retune the model on these outcomes and then call the same data an untouched test set.

title: Combining study results
objective: Explain inverse-variance weighting and decide whether a pooled effect answers a coherent question.
summary: Pooling requires comparable populations, contrasts, outcomes and follow-up, together with an assessment of bias and dependence. Inverse-variance weights favour more precise estimates. A fixed-effect illustration assumes a common underlying effect. Random-effects models allow between-study variation but cannot repair biased studies or justify combining incompatible questions.
challenge: Three studies estimate the same risk difference, but one has twice the standard error of the others. Should it receive twice the weight, half the weight or a quarter of the weight?
steps: The fictional independent studies report one-year adverse-outcome risk differences (programme minus control) of −0.04, −0.08 and −0.03, with SEs 0.02, 0.04 and 0.02. In Summary meta-analysis choose Risk Difference, then Standard Error, and select the two named columns; use default study labels and 95% confidence. Compare the fixed-effect estimate with R: −4 percentage points, with a 95% normal interval of about −6.6 to −1.4 percentage points. Both use the inverse-variance common-effect estimate and a normal critical value. The R output retains unrounded values. This exercise assumes approximately normal estimates and a common underlying effect; it is not a complete systematic review.
r:
# Three fictional independent trials: same adverse outcome and one-year horizon.
# Risk difference = programme minus control. SE, not SD, is supplied.
effect <- c(-0.04,-0.08,-0.03); se <- c(0.02,0.04,0.02)
weight <- 1/se^2
pooled <- sum(weight*effect)/sum(weight)
pooled_se <- sqrt(1/sum(weight))
pooled_ci <- pooled+c(-1,1)*qnorm(0.975)*pooled_se
q <- sum(weight*(effect-pooled)^2)
print(data.frame(Study=1:3,Risk_difference=effect,SE=se,Percent_weight=100*weight/sum(weight)))
print(c(Pooled=pooled,SE=pooled_se,Lower=pooled_ci[1],Upper=pooled_ci[2],Q=q))
lower <- effect-qnorm(0.975)*se; upper <- effect+qnorm(0.975)*se
plot(effect,1:3,pch=19,xlim=range(c(lower,upper,0)),ylim=c(0,3.5),yaxt="n",xlab="Risk difference: programme minus control",ylab="",main="Fictional fixed-effect illustration")
segments(lower,1:3,upper,1:3); abline(v=0,lty=2)
points(pooled,0,pch=18); segments(pooled_ci[1],0,pooled_ci[2],0)
axis(2,at=0:3,labels=c("Pooled","Study 1","Study 2","Study 3"),las=1)
# The interval estimates a common effect under the model; not a prediction interval.
# Few studies give weak information about heterogeneity and publication bias.

# Optional further learning: conventional Q-based I-squared.
# Change FALSE to TRUE to run this extension after the main lesson.
if (FALSE) {
  study_df <- length(effect)-1
  i_squared <- if(q>0) 100*max(0,(q-study_df)/q) else 0
  print(c(Q=q,df=study_df,I_squared_percent=i_squared))
  # Here I-squared is 0%, after truncating a negative untruncated estimate.
  # Three studies give little information: 0% does not establish homogeneity.
  # Do not select fixed versus random effects just from Q's P value or I-squared.
}

title: Describing and displaying data
objective: Match a summary and display to what was measured and how the sample was obtained.
summary: Classify a variable before analysing it. Blood group is nominal, symptom grade is ordinal, visits are discrete counts, and waiting time is continuous even when recorded to whole minutes. Use counts and percentages with explicit denominators for categories. For a roughly symmetric quantitative distribution, the mean and standard deviation describe centre and spread. For skewed data, the median and interquartile range (IQR) are resistant to extreme values. Inspect a histogram or dot plot first; a box plot compactly compares groups. A histogram groups quantitative values into bins; a bar chart compares categories. A sampling frame defines who can be reached, and non-response can bias a probability sample. A normal model may describe approximately symmetric continuous measurements; a binomial model counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials with the same probability, and a Poisson model can describe event counts over fixed exposure when conditions such as a constant rate and independent increments are reasonable.
challenge: Which summary would you lead with if describing a typical wait? What would you add to show that some people wait much longer?
steps: Enter the eight fictional wait times in one column and run Univariate Summary. Check the histogram or dot plot, median and mean. Seven waits are 18 minutes or less and one is 42 minutes. The median is 11.5 minutes and the mean is 15.75. R's default quartiles give Q1 = 10 and Q3 = 15, for an IQR of 5 minutes. Small-sample quartile conventions can differ, so state the method if results differ.

wait <- c(9, 10, 10, 11, 12, 14, 18, 42)
stopifnot(mean(wait) == 15.75, median(wait) == 11.5, IQR(wait) == 5)
print(c(mean = mean(wait), median = median(wait), sd = sd(wait), IQR = IQR(wait)))
hist(wait, breaks = seq(5, 45, 5), xlab = "Wait in minutes", main = "Fictional clinic waiting times")
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(pbinom(0, 10, 0.2), 0.8^10)), isTRUE(all.equal(dpois(0, 2), exp(-2))))

title: Choosing a statistical test
objective: Select an analysis using the outcome type, design, target effect and plausible assumptions.
summary: Start with the scientific question and the outcome scale. For quantitative outcomes, a paired analysis works on within-pair information; a paired t test targets the mean of paired differences and relies on independent pairs, with normal differences for exact small-sample inference. For two independent samples targeting a mean difference, Welch's t test allows unequal variances. Consider plots, outliers, sample size and the intended estimand before choosing a rank or sign method. Wilcoxon signed-rank relies on symmetric difference distributions for the usual location interpretation. Mann–Whitney compares distributions or rank tendencies under an appropriate sampling design; equal shape is needed for the familiar location-shift interpretation. For independent counts, Pearson's chi-square uses expected counts under the null; Fisher's exact test is a usual choice for sparse 2×2 tables. Binary matched outcomes need a paired method such as McNemar based on discordant pairs. Pearson correlation describes linear association; Spearman describes monotonic association using ranks. Inspect a scatterplot for curvature, outliers and dependence. Correlation alone does not establish agreement or causation.
challenge: Your independent groups have a continuous outcome with very different spreads and strong right skew. What effect would answer the practical question, and what further checks guide the analysis?
steps: Enter the fictional before and after measurements in two columns, select both and run Paired t to estimate mean improvement. The eight differences average 2.625 units. Check their spread and the interval before interpreting the point estimate. Then compare the expected counts and Fisher result from a separate independent 2×2 example in R. Observe that equal-looking columns are not themselves evidence of pairing.
r:
before <- c(20, 21, 22, 19, 24, 23, 25, 21)
after <- c(20, 20, 20, 17, 21, 19, 21, 16)
paired <- t.test(before, after, paired = TRUE)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(unname(paired$estimate), 21/8)))
print(paired)
counts <- matrix(c(0, 4, 5, 3), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
pearson <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(counts, correct = FALSE))
exact <- fisher.test(counts)
support <- 0:4
null_prob <- dhyper(support, 5, 7, 4)
stopifnot(min(pearson$expected) < 5, isTRUE(all.equal(exact$p.value, sum(null_prob[null_prob <= null_prob[1] + 1e-12]))))
print(pearson$expected)
print(exact)

title: Surveillance and outbreak investigation
topic: Person, place, time and changing denominators
objective: Interpret a surveillance signal and design a transparent first comparison of possible outbreak exposures.
summary: Surveillance tracks health patterns for public-health action. Define the case, population, place, time and coverage. Compare equivalent periods, checking reporting delays, seasonality, testing and who is at risk. Sentinel sites can track trends without representing the whole population. Use a line list and plot onsets in an epidemic curve. Compare attack rates in a defined attendee cohort. A case-control study can help assess exposures when the population at risk cannot be counted. Direct standardisation applies shared weights to stratum-specific rates. Indirect standardisation compares observed cases with expected cases based on reference rates. The ecological fallacy is inferring individual associations from group averages. Time trends can reflect concurrent events or serial dependence.
challenge: A larger number of positive laboratory reports appears after a new testing centre opens. What denominators, time patterns and independent sources would help tell whether occurrence changed?
steps: Among 120 fictional event attendees, 18 of 60 who ate a dish and six of 60 who did not became ill during follow-up. In prospective risk analysis, use case counts 18 and 6, non-case counts 42 and 54, with exposed then unexposed columns. Attack rates are 30% and 10%, so the risk ratio is 3 and the difference is 20 percentage points. The overall attack rate is 24/120 = 20%. Two of those 24 cases died from the illness within 30 days of onset, giving 30-day case fatality of 8.3%. Check timing and co-exposures before attributing the outbreak. R also compares crude with directly standardised rates in separate data.
r:
ill <- c(18, 6)
attendees <- c(60, 60)
risk <- ill/attendees
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(risk[1]/risk[2], 3)), isTRUE(all.equal(diff(rev(risk)), 0.2)))
# The two denominators answer different questions.
attack_rate <- sum(ill) / sum(attendees)
case_fatality_30d <- 2 / sum(ill)
stopifnot(abs(attack_rate - .20) < 1e-12,
          abs(case_fatality_30d - 1/12) < 1e-12)
print(c(attack_exposed = risk[1], attack_unexposed = risk[2], risk_ratio = risk[1]/risk[2],
        overall_attack_rate = attack_rate, case_fatality_30d = case_fatality_30d))
age_rates <- matrix(c(1, 8, 2, 6), nrow = 2, dimnames = list(c("Younger","Older"), c("A","B")))
weights <- c(0.75, 0.25)
adjusted <- drop(crossprod(weights, age_rates))
crude <- colSums(age_rates * cbind(c(0.25, 0.75), c(0.8, 0.2)))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(unname(adjusted), c(2.75, 3))), isTRUE(all.equal(unname(crude), c(6.25, 2.8))))
print(rbind(crude = crude, direct_standardised = adjusted))

title: Repeated, clustered and survey data
topic: What the sample design does to uncertainty
objective: Identify the independent unit and use the dependence, sampling and weighting design when estimating precision.
summary: Repeated measurements from the same person and participants within the same school, clinic or household can be correlated. In cluster-randomised studies the clusters, not the participant rows, were randomised. A paired change is useful for exactly two comparable observations per person; mixed models, suitable marginal methods, cluster summaries or design-based analysis may be needed for more complex settings. Survey strata are subgroups sampled separately and can improve precision; survey clusters are sampled groups containing multiple units. Inverse selection-probability weights account for unequal selection chances, with further adjustment where justified. Variance estimation also needs the strata, primary sampling units and weights, or provided replicate weights. For a simple equal-size cluster design with common intracluster correlation rho, the approximate design effect relative to the same number of independent observations is 1 + (m − 1)rho. This is a variance ratio; multiply a simple-random-sample standard error by its square root. Unequal cluster sizes, sampling weights and few clusters require more careful methods.
challenge: A survey uses unequal selection probabilities and samples people within households. What variables do you need to estimate a population proportion and its uncertainty?
steps: Consider a fictional equal-size cluster sample of 20 clinics with 15 patients each. With ICC 0.10 the simple design effect is 2.4; the rough effective sample size is 300/2.4 = 125. If the estimate of event risk is 0.20, the simple independent-binomial SE is about 0.023 and the inflation gives about 0.036. This is a design illustration; real survey analyses use the actual structure. In a separate weighting example, equal-sized samples from two strata with population shares 80% and 20% and risks 10% and 30% give an estimated population risk of 14%, versus an unweighted 20%.
r:
clusters <- 20
m <- 15
rho <- 0.10
n <- clusters*m
deff <- 1 + (m - 1)*rho
p <- 0.2
simple_se <- sqrt(p*(1-p)/n)
effective_n <- n/deff
adjusted_se <- simple_se*sqrt(deff)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(deff, 2.4)), isTRUE(all.equal(effective_n, 125)), isTRUE(all.equal(adjusted_se, sqrt(0.16/125))))
print(c(n = n, design_effect = deff, effective_n = effective_n, naive_se = simple_se, adjusted_se = adjusted_se))
stratum_risk <- c(0.1, 0.3)
population_share <- c(0.8, 0.2)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(sum(stratum_risk*population_share), 0.14)), isTRUE(all.equal(mean(stratum_risk), 0.2)))
print(c(weighted = sum(stratum_risk*population_share), unweighted = mean(stratum_risk)))

title: Planning power and interpreting trial margins
objective: Plan an independent two-arm superiority trial and distinguish its decision rules from noninferiority and equivalence.
summary: Choose the outcome, clinically important difference, plausible variability, allocation, significance level and target power before recruitment. Type I error is rejection under a true null. Type II error is failure to reject at a specified alternative. Power is one minus that probability. A sample size is conditional on the design and assumptions, not a guarantee of a positive result. Use prespecified clinical margins to interpret noninferiority and equivalence.
challenge: A report says two treatments are equivalent because its two-sided P value is 0.24. What prespecified margin, confidence interval and design information would you ask for?
steps: A fictional parallel trial targets a 4-point difference in a symptom improvement score with a common within-group SD of 10. Higher scores mean greater improvement. For independent participants, equal groups, a two-sided 5% test and 90% power at that difference, the equal-variance two-sample t calculation needs 133 analysable participants per arm. If 10% are expected to be unavailable, ceil(133/0.90) gives 148 per arm for recruitment. This allowance does not remove bias from missing outcomes. Halving the detectable difference to 2 points increases the target to 527 analysable participants per arm. In a separate illustrative trial, new minus control improvement is +1.4 with a 95% interval about −0.36 to +3.16. If −2.5 is the justified noninferiority boundary and the prespecified one-sided alpha is 0.025, the lower limit clears that boundary. The interval crosses zero, so it does not establish superiority. Its upper end also exceeds +2.5, so it fails a rule requiring the entire 95% interval within ±2.5. In StatsDirect choose equal groups (one control per experimental participant), SD 10, difference 4, 90% power and two-sided 5% significance. Allow for anticipated missing outcomes separately. The equivalence rule above is illustrative. Conventional two one-sided tests at 5% use a 90% two-sided interval.
r:
# Fictional planning model for an equal-variance two-sample t test
n_for <- function(delta) ceiling(power.t.test(delta = delta, sd = 10,
    sig.level = 0.05, power = 0.90, type = "two.sample",
    alternative = "two.sided", strict = TRUE)$n)
n <- n_for(4)
recruit <- ceiling(n / 0.90)
print(c(analysable_per_arm = n, recruit_per_arm = recruit,
        smaller_effect_per_arm = n_for(2)))
stopifnot(n == 133L, recruit == 148L, n_for(2) == 527L)
# Illustrative normal interval from a different, already completed trial
estimate <- 1.4
se <- 0.9
ci <- estimate + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * se
margin <- 2.5
print(ci)
stopifnot(ci[1] > -margin, ci[1] < 0, ci[2] > margin)

learningObjectives: Identify the inputs and assumptions for a two-sample sample size calculation.
Describe type I and type II errors without reversing conditional probabilities.

keyConcepts.explanation: With a fixed sample and test, power depends on the true effect and variability. Smaller meaningful effects, greater SD or stricter alpha usually require more participants.

When higher is better, rule out an unacceptable loss by placing the lower confidence limit above the prespecified negative margin. An effective active control and a trial able to distinguish effective from ineffective treatment underpin interpretation.

Both bounds must lie within justified margins at the confidence level specified for the test. For two one-sided tests at 5% each, use the corresponding 90% two-sided interval. Here the stated rule uses a 95% interval.

In noninferiority trials, deviations and crossover can dilute differences. Check the prespecified estimand and supporting analysis sets, including per-protocol sensitivity analyses when appropriate. Agreement across analyses helps but cannot rescue poor trial conduct.

misconceptions.claim: Power of 90% means the treatment is 90% likely to work.
misconceptions.correction: It is the chance of rejecting a null under a specified true effect and model in repeated trials.

misconceptions.claim: A nonsignificant superiority test proves equivalence.
misconceptions.correction: It can leave worthwhile benefits or harms compatible with the data. Equivalence needs justified margins and an interval narrow enough to exclude both.

workedExample.design: Independent equal-sized arms and common SD for planning. A separate completed-trial example uses an approximate normal interval and a 2.5-point prechosen margin.
workedExample.interpretation: Plan for 133 analysable or 148 recruited participants per arm at 4 points. In the separate example, conclude noninferiority only if the margin, estimand, active-control evidence and conduct support that inference.

teachingPrompts.prompt: Would a 95% interval of −1 to +1 establish superiority, noninferiority or equivalence under the stated rules?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: It crosses zero and satisfies both margin criteria. Whether those claims are justified also depends on the design and prespecified tests.

title: Reading a clinical trial beyond its abstract
objective: Trace a trial from enrolment to analysis and judge whether its effect estimate answers the clinical question.
summary: A random sequence generates assignments. Allocation concealment keeps the next assignment unknown during enrolment. Blinding limits knowledge after allocation. For a treatment-policy comparison, follow participants in their assigned groups even after stopping treatment. An intention-to-treat label does not resolve unobserved outcomes. Compare the abstract against registration, protocol, participant flow and analysis. Check whether the endpoint matters directly to patients or is a surrogate.
challenge: An abstract says a new care pathway reduced relapses in treatment completers. Which three details would you request before advising a service to change practice?
steps: In a fictional parallel trial, 120 people are randomised per arm. Relapses occur in 18 of 100 observed people assigned the pathway and 24 of 114 observed controls. The observed risk difference is −3.1 percentage points. Assigning all missing pathway outcomes and no missing controls as events gives +11.7 points. Reversing the assignments gives −10.0 points. These are bounds based on extreme scenarios. Check missingness, assessor masking, endpoint and protocol. Weigh absolute effects, uncertainty, harms and applicability. Ward randomisation requires accounting for clustering. In crossover trials compare within people and assess period effects, washout and carryover.
r:
# Fictional relapse counts, following original group allocation
randomised <- c(pathway = 120, usual_care = 120)
observed <- c(pathway = 100, usual_care = 114)
events <- c(pathway = 18, usual_care = 24)
missing <- randomised - observed
rd <- function(risks) unname(risks[1] - risks[2])
observed_rd <- rd(events / observed)
favourable_rd <- rd((events + c(0, missing[2])) / randomised)
unfavourable_rd <- rd((events + c(missing[1], 0)) / randomised)
print(c(available_case_RD = observed_rd, best_for_pathway = favourable_rd,
        worst_for_pathway = unfavourable_rd))
stopifnot(abs(observed_rd - (18/100 - 24/114)) < 1e-12,
          abs(favourable_rd + 0.10) < 1e-12,
          abs(unfavourable_rd - 14/120) < 1e-12)

learningObjectives: Distinguish sequence generation, concealment and blinding.

keyConcepts.explanation: Protect enrolment from foreknowledge of the next assignment. Secure central allocation is one way. A computer-generated list alone cannot conceal assignments if recruiters can see it.
Document who knew the assignments and when. Masking outcome assessors can limit assessment bias even when patients and clinicians cannot be masked.

Define whose outcomes, the endpoint and time, the treatment contrast and how to handle events like stopping or switching therapy. State how missing outcomes are addressed and test sensitivity to assumptions.

How people feel, function or survive can be measured directly. A surrogate, such as a laboratory marker, stands in for a clinical outcome and needs evidence that intervention effects on the marker predict effects on that outcome in context. Prognostic association alone is insufficient.
People in the same randomised ward are likely correlated. Outcomes from different treatment periods in one person are paired. Carryover can confuse a crossover effect even with the correct pairing.

misconceptions.claim: Randomisation makes all later exclusions harmless.
misconceptions.correction: Exclusions and outcome loss after allocation can undermine comparability.

misconceptions.claim: Reporting CONSORT items establishes low risk of bias.
misconceptions.correction: Good reporting shows what was done and enables appraisal. It cannot replace sound conduct.

title: Using likelihood ratios and evaluating diagnostic thresholds
objective: Update a pretest probability with a likelihood ratio and judge whether diagnostic study results apply to the patient.
summary: Bayes’ theorem updates pretest odds using the likelihood ratio for the result. The likelihood ratio compares how often that result occurs in people with and without the target condition. Multiply pretest odds by the ratio and convert back to probability. A receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve displays sensitivity and the false-positive proportion across thresholds. Before applying an estimate, check the reference standard, who received it and whether the study patients resemble the intended population.
challenge: A test's sensitivity is reported as 95% in a sample of severe cases and healthy volunteers. What additional evidence would you need before using that estimate in a general practice population with uncertain diagnoses?
steps: Use fictional marker scores for people with (1, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9) and without (0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 5) the condition. Higher values suggest disease. At a positive threshold of at least 4, sensitivity and specificity are both 80%. LR+ = 0.80/0.20 = 4 and LR− = 0.20/0.80 = 0.25. With a separate, clinically justified pretest probability of 20%, odds are 1:4. A positive result raises probability to 50%, and a negative result lowers it to about 5.9%. At threshold 5, sensitivity drops to 60% and specificity rises to 90%. Plot the thresholds and connect these changes to the harms of missed diagnoses and unnecessary follow-up. The small sample teaches arithmetic. It cannot establish a reliable clinical threshold. In StatsDirect select one ROC series, then choose Condition present at the first column prompt and Condition absent at the next. Compare the AUC and use the R exercise to calculate likelihood ratios at a specified threshold.
r:
# Fictional independent test results, with known condition status
disease <- c(1,3,4,4,5,5,6,7,8,9)
no_disease <- c(0,1,1,2,2,3,3,3,4,5)
thresholds <- c(Inf, sort(unique(c(disease, no_disease)), decreasing = TRUE))
roc <- data.frame(threshold = thresholds,
  sensitivity = sapply(thresholds, function(t) mean(disease >= t)),
  specificity = sapply(thresholds, function(t) mean(no_disease < t)))
at4 <- subset(roc, threshold == 4)
at5 <- subset(roc, threshold == 5)
lr <- c(positive = at4$sensitivity / (1 - at4$specificity),
        negative = (1 - at4$sensitivity) / at4$specificity)
pretest_odds <- 0.20 / 0.80
posttest_odds <- lr * pretest_odds
posttest_probability <- posttest_odds / (1 + posttest_odds)
auc <- mean(outer(disease, no_disease, function(a, b) (a > b) + 0.5*(a == b)))
print(roc)
print(posttest_probability)
print(c(AUC = auc))
stopifnot(abs(lr[1] - 4) < 1e-12, abs(lr[2] - 0.25) < 1e-12,
          max(abs(posttest_probability - c(0.5, 1/17))) < 1e-12,
          at5$sensitivity == 0.6, at5$specificity == 0.9, abs(auc - 0.845) < 1e-12)

learningObjectives: Apply Bayes’ theorem in odds form to update a pretest probability.
Read ROC coordinates and interpret what AUC measures.
Recognise spectrum and verification problems and communicate uncertainty.

keyConcepts.explanation: Post-test odds = pretest odds × likelihood ratio. For a binary result, LR+ = sensitivity / (1 − specificity) and LR− = (1 − sensitivity) / specificity. Use both parts of each ratio from the same threshold and relevant population.

keyConcepts.term: ROC and area under the curve (AUC)
keyConcepts.explanation: A point gives sensitivity against 1 − specificity. The empirical AUC here is 0.845, the probability of a randomly selected case score exceeding a randomly selected noncase score, counting ties as halves. It does not set the clinical threshold.
Severity, comorbidity and setting can change accuracy. If the reference diagnosis is obtained mainly in test-positive participants, estimates based only on those verified can be biased.

Describe the estimated chance in context, relate it to possible next steps and explain the limitations. For this illustration, about 50 of 100 similar people with a positive result would have the condition if the estimates apply.

misconceptions.claim: An LR of four means a 20% chance becomes 80%.
misconceptions.correction: The LR multiplies odds. Here a positive result moves 20% to 50%.

misconceptions.claim: A high AUC tells us which cut-off maximises patient benefit.
misconceptions.correction: AUC describes ranking across thresholds. Consequences of errors, prevalence, preferences and costs inform the chosen cut-off.

workedExample.design: Two equal-sized illustrative score groups with complete reference status. The 20% pretest estimate is supplied separately because the artificial 50:50 study case mix does not describe clinical prevalence.
workedExample.interpretation: A positive at threshold 4 gives 50% under the stated assumptions. A negative leaves residual risk. Describe that uncertainty without labelling either result diagnostic.

teachingPrompts.prompt: Would you say that a negative result rules the condition out?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: No. State the remaining probability and why the next step depends on the clinical context.

teachingPrompts.prompt: If the reference standard is applied mainly to those testing positive, which entries in the diagnostic table become uncertain?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: Disease and nondisease status among unverified negative results are unknown. Complete-case sensitivity and specificity may be biased. The direction and size depend on the verification process.

rProgression.bridge: Match sensitivity and false-positive fractions to threshold points. Use the R calculation to update the odds at one point. The ROC example deliberately has equal numbers with and without the condition. Its predictive values reflect that artificial case mix. For the clinical scenario, start from the stated 20% pretest probability.
rProgression.coding: Change the pretest probability separately from the threshold and explain what each change affects.

title: Evaluating a screening programme
objective: Judge screening on outcomes in the population offered it and compare benefits, harms and participation using appropriate denominators.
summary: A screening programme offers a pathway to an eligible population. Follow invitations, uptake, results, diagnosis and management through to outcomes. Counting additional diagnoses or comparing survival after diagnosis can exaggerate benefit. To estimate the effect of offering screening, compare outcomes by assigned invitation group where randomised evidence is available. Also measure harms, including false alarms, overdiagnosis and unnecessary treatment. For antenatal screening, enabling an informed personal choice may itself be a programme goal.
challenge: A prenatal programme reports higher uptake and more detected cases. What additional outcomes, decisions and denominators do you need before deciding whether access and informed choice improved?
steps: In a fictional ten-year invitation trial, 40,000 people are assigned an invitation and 40,000 usual care. There are 80 and 100 deaths from the target condition. Compare all assigned people, giving 2.0 versus 2.5 deaths per 1,000 and a difference of −0.5 per 1,000. The point estimate is 20 fewer deaths per 40,000 invited. An approximate interval in R includes zero. Among 30,000 invited people who attend, 600 screen positive and all have known follow-up status. Of those, 120 have the target condition and 480 do not. The proportion of positive results confirmed is 120/600 = 20%. There were 480 false-positive results per 30,000 attendees, or 16 per 1,000. Check harms in both groups, including downstream procedures and overdiagnosis. These false-positive counts do not measure overdiagnosis.
r:
# Fictional trial, equal complete follow-up from random assignment
deaths <- c(invited = 80, usual_care = 100)
n <- c(invited = 40000, usual_care = 40000)
p <- deaths / n
rd <- unname(p[1] - p[2])
se <- sqrt(sum(p * (1 - p) / n))
ci <- rd + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * se
print(1000 * c(p, risk_difference = rd, lower = ci[1], upper = ci[2]))
positive <- 600
confirmed <- 120
attended <- 30000
ppv <- confirmed / positive
false_positive_per_1000 <- 1000 * (positive - confirmed) / attended
print(c(PPV = ppv, false_positive_per_1000 = false_positive_per_1000))
# Separate fictional maternity indicators for the same period and geography
live_births <- 40000
stillbirths <- 120
early_neonatal_deaths <- 40
maternal_deaths <- 3
maternal_ratio <- 1e5 * maternal_deaths / live_births
perinatal_rate <- 1000 * (stillbirths + early_neonatal_deaths) / (live_births + stillbirths)
print(c(maternal_per_100000_live_births = maternal_ratio,
        perinatal_per_1000_total_births = perinatal_rate))
stopifnot(abs(rd + .0005) < 1e-12, ci[1] < 0, ci[2] > 0, ppv == .2,
          false_positive_per_1000 == 16, maternal_ratio == 7.5,
          round(perinatal_rate, 2) == 3.99)

learningObjectives: Distinguish lead-time, length bias and overdiagnosis.
Compare population outcomes by invitation and report downstream harms with denominators.
Explain informed choice and distinguish maternal and perinatal indicators.

keyConcepts.explanation: Earlier diagnosis adds time measured from diagnosis even when death occurs at the same time. Screening also preferentially finds conditions with a longer detectable preclinical phase. Both can improve observed survival from diagnosis without demonstrating that screening postpones death.

Overdiagnosis identifies real disease that would not have become symptomatic or caused harm in that person without screening. A false positive is an abnormal screening result when the target condition is absent.

Review whether eligible pregnant people can make an informed decision, understand a higher-chance result and access appropriate follow-up. Report offer, uptake, diagnostic follow-up and meaningful outcomes separately. There is no single desirable uptake rate that establishes informed choice.

The WHO maternal mortality ratio uses maternal deaths in the defined time window per 100,000 live births. The ONS perinatal mortality rate combines stillbirths and deaths under 7 days per 1,000 total births, using its defined birth and gestation criteria. Early neonatal mortality uses live births. title: Time to event and competing risks
topic: Risk sets, competing events and survival comparisons
objective: Choose an event definition, time origin and estimator that match the question.
summary: Define the start of follow-up, event and censoring. A right-censored participant contributes observed time at risk. Kaplan–Meier multiplies conditional probabilities of remaining free of the specified event. Find the median from where the estimated curve reaches or drops below 0.50. If it stays above 0.50, the median has not been reached. Death before relapse prevents first relapse and enters its real-world cumulative incidence as a competing event. Log-rank compares curves using observed and expected event counts. A Cox hazard ratio describes relative instantaneous event rates. Its usual constant summary assumes proportional hazards.
challenge: After cancer treatment, how does death before relapse differ from ending observation at the last known relapse-free visit?
steps: In the fictional oncology data, use Analysis → Survival Analysis → Kaplan–Meier. Select Time (months), Composite event (1 = relapse or death before relapse, 0 = censored) and use Arm to identify the two groups. Usual care is Arm 0. Compare its composite event-free estimate at month 4 with R's 4/9. The curve first drops past 50% at month 4, so its median composite event-free time is four months. For relapse alone use the R calculation with Event type (0 = censored, 1 = relapse, 2 = death before relapse). It gives relapse cumulative incidence 7/18. Censoring deaths and taking 1 minus Kaplan–Meier instead gives 4/9. Both comparisons use a deliberately tiny dataset.
r:
# Fictional first-event oncology follow-up. 0=censored, 1=relapse, 2=death before relapse.
time <- c(1:6, seq(1.5,6.5))
kind <- c(1,2,0,1,2,0, 2,1,0,2,0,0)
arm <- rep(0:1,each=6)
any_event <- kind != 0
t <- time[arm==0]; k <- kind[arm==0]
et <- sort(t[k!=0])
n <- vapply(et,function(u) sum(t>=u),integer(1))
d1 <- vapply(et,function(u) sum(t==u & k==1),integer(1))
d2 <- vapply(et,function(u) sum(t==u & k==2),integer(1))
event_free <- cumprod(1-(d1+d2)/n)
before <- c(1,head(event_free,-1))
relapse <- cumsum(before*d1/n)
death <- cumsum(before*d2/n)
naive <- 1-cumprod(1-d1/n)
i <- match(4,et)
stopifnot(all.equal(event_free+relapse+death,rep(1,length(et))),
          abs(event_free[i]-4/9)<1e-12, abs(relapse[i]-7/18)<1e-12,
          abs(naive[i]-4/9)<1e-12)
print(data.frame(month=et, at_risk=n, event_free, relapse, death, naive))
# The step crosses 0.5 at an event in this example, with no plateau at 0.5.
stopifnot(event_free[i-1] > .5, event_free[i] < .5)
print(c(median_event_free_months = et[i]))
# Composite endpoint. This teaching partial likelihood has no ties.
events <- sort(time[any_event])
n0 <- vapply(events,function(u) sum(time>=u & arm==0),integer(1))
n1 <- vapply(events,function(u) sum(time>=u & arm==1),integer(1))
o1 <- sum(arm[any_event])
chi <- (o1-sum(n1/(n0+n1)))^2/sum(n0*n1/(n0+n1)^2)
p <- pchisq(chi,1,lower.tail=FALSE)
log_likelihood <- function(beta) beta*o1-sum(log(n0+n1*exp(beta)))
hr <- exp(optimize(log_likelihood,c(-10,10),maximum=TRUE)$maximum)
stopifnot(abs(chi-.2832613)<1e-6,abs(p-.5945716)<1e-6,abs(hr-.6670618)<1e-4)
print(c(logrank=chi,p_value=p,composite_HR=hr))
plot(c(0,et,6),c(0,relapse,tail(relapse,1)),type="s",ylim=c(0,1),
     xlab="Months after treatment",ylab="Cumulative incidence",main="Fictional usual-care cohort")
lines(c(0,et,6),c(0,death,tail(death,1)),type="s",lty=2)
legend("topleft",c("First relapse","Death before relapse"),lty=1:2,bty="n")

keyConcepts.explanation: The event has not been recorded by the last observed event-free time. Censoring removes a person from later risk sets without causing a Kaplan–Meier drop. Follow-up losses associated with prognosis can bias estimates.

Read the 0.50 crossing on the step curve for the defined event. When a step jumps across 0.50, use the event time. StatsDirect and R use the midpoint for a plateau exactly at 0.50 between successive event times. The last censored time alone does not give a median.
Sum observed versus expected events across risk sets. The test is especially sensitive under proportional hazards and can miss opposing early and late differences.
Compare instantaneous rates among those still at risk at the same time with specified covariates fixed. Inspect time patterns, such as scaled Schoenfeld residuals, before relying on a constant ratio.

Aalen–Johansen adds each cause's event increment weighted by the probability of remaining free of every first event just beforehand. A cause-specific hazard ratio alone does not determine cumulative incidence.

title: Choosing and interpreting regression models
objective: Choose a model for the outcome and explain what an adjusted coefficient means.
summary: Linear regression models a mean in the outcome's units, logistic regression models log odds for a binary outcome, and a Poisson model with a log exposure offset models a count rate. Adjust for selected covariates using the design and subject knowledge. Assess functional form, residuals, uncertainty and, for prediction, calibration beyond the development fit.
challenge: A new respiratory protocol is used more often for severe patients. How could a crude comparison obscure an association within levels of severity?
steps: Use Analysis → Regression and Correlation → Logistic with four fictional strata. Choose Grouped response data and include an intercept, with weighting off. Use Total as the number assessed, Events as the number who reattend, and Protocol and Severe as 0/1 predictors. The adjusted protocol odds ratio is 0.50, compared with about 0.85 when severity is omitted. Find the reference levels and interval. The R script also uses separate datasets for recovery days and counts accumulated over person-time. For the protocol odds ratio, base R gives a profile-likelihood 95% interval of about 0.331 to 0.748. It also shows the Wald interval (about 0.333 to 0.751) for comparison. Compare methods as well as endpoints.
r:
# Fictional respiratory service examples. Each model has its own outcome.
g <- data.frame(protocol=c(0,0,1,1),severe=c(0,1,0,1),total=c(200,100,90,210),events=c(40,50,10,70))
logistic <- glm(cbind(events,total-events)~protocol+severe,binomial(),g)
crude <- glm(cbind(events,total-events)~protocol,binomial(),g)
lr <- coef(logistic)["protocol"]
wald <- exp(lr+c(-1,1)*qnorm(.975)*sqrt(vcov(logistic)["protocol","protocol"]))
stopifnot(abs(exp(lr)-.5)<1e-8,abs(exp(coef(crude)["protocol"])-(80/220)/(90/210))<1e-8)
print(c(adjusted_OR=unname(exp(lr)),crude_OR=unname(exp(coef(crude)["protocol"])),Wald_lower=wald[1],Wald_upper=wald[2]))
no <- predict(logistic,transform(g,protocol=0),type="response")
yes <- predict(logistic,transform(g,protocol=1),type="response")
profile <- exp(confint(logistic, parm="protocol"))
stopifnot(all(abs(profile-c(.3312941,.7478764))<1e-6))
print(profile)
rd <- weighted.mean(yes-no,g$total)
stopifnot(abs(rd-((1/9-1/5)*290+(1/3-1/2)*310)/600)<1e-8)
print(c(standardised_probability_difference=rd))
days <- data.frame(protocol=rep(g$protocol,each=2),severe=rep(g$severe,each=2),days=c(5,7,9,11,3,5,7,9))
linear <- lm(days~protocol+severe,days)
stopifnot(abs(coef(linear)["protocol"]+2)<1e-10)
print(coef(summary(linear)))
rates <- transform(g,episodes=c(10,18,8,18),person_months=c(200,120,240,180))
rate <- glm(episodes~protocol+severe+offset(log(person_months)),poisson(),rates)
stopifnot(abs(exp(coef(rate)["protocol"])-2/3)<1e-8)
print(exp(coef(rate)))
# Fixed probabilities evaluated in a separate fictional population.
pred <- c(.2,.5,.8); n <- c(100,100,100); observed <- c(15,40,70)
stopifnot(abs(sum(observed)/sum(n)-125/300)<1e-12,weighted.mean(pred,n)==.5)
print(data.frame(predicted=pred,observed=observed/n))
plot(pred,observed/n,xlim=c(0,1),ylim=c(0,1),pch=19,
     xlab="Predicted probability",ylab="Observed proportion",main="Fictional model validation")
abline(0,1,lty=2)

title: Do two measurements agree?
topic: Bland–Altman limits, kappa and intraclass correlation
objective: Choose an agreement measure for the scale, and decide what size of disagreement matters clinically.
summary: Correlation measures association. Two devices can rank patients almost identically and still give differences large enough to change care. For paired quantitative measures, inspect differences against their means and compare the limits of agreement with a prespecified acceptable range. For two categorical raters report the agreement table and observed agreement alongside Cohen's kappa. For quantitative reliability specify the ICC design, single or average rating, and whether absolute agreement or consistency matters.
challenge: Two paediatric respiratory devices have near-perfect correlation. What else would you need before replacing one with the other?
steps: In the fictional data, enter Reference reading and New reading from the same eight children. Select Analysis → Parametric → Paired t and request agreement analysis. With Reference selected first, StatsDirect uses Reference minus New: a mean of −2.5 units and limits around −4.84 and −0.16 units. The R script uses New minus Reference. Mean difference is +2.5 units and the usual 95% limits are about +0.16 and +4.84 units. The upper limit exceeds the example's prespecified ±3 tolerance. The separate R examples use a classification table for Cohen's kappa and an ANOVA decomposition for two single-measure ICCs. The illustrative sample is too small for an interchangeability decision.
r:
# One fictional pair per child, on the same measurement scale.
reference <- c(19,26,31,38,43,51,57,64)
new <- c(20,28,34,40,47,52,60,68)
mid <- (new+reference)/2
difference <- new-reference
bias <- mean(difference)
loa <- bias+c(-1,1)*1.96*sd(difference)
stopifnot(bias==2.5,all(abs(loa-c(.1573519,4.8426481))<1e-6),cor(reference,new)>.99)
print(c(correlation=cor(reference,new),bias=bias,lower=loa[1],upper=loa[2]))
plot(mid,difference,pch=19,ylim=range(c(difference,loa,-3,3)),
     xlab="Pair mean",ylab="New minus reference",main="Fictional device agreement")
abline(h=bias)
abline(h=loa,lty=2)
abline(h=c(-3,3),lty=3)
legend("bottomright",c("Mean difference","Limits of agreement","Clinical tolerance"),lty=1:3,bty="n")

# Separate nominal ratings from 100 fictional encounters.
ratings <- matrix(c(36,4,8,52),2,byrow=TRUE)
p_observed <- sum(diag(ratings))/sum(ratings)
p_expected <- sum(rowSums(ratings)*colSums(ratings))/sum(ratings)^2
kappa <- (p_observed-p_expected)/(1-p_expected)
stopifnot(p_observed==.88,abs(p_expected-.512)<1e-12,abs(kappa-(.88-.512)/(1-.512))<1e-12)
print(c(observed_agreement=p_observed,expected_agreement=p_expected,kappa=kappa))

# Balanced two-way ANOVA, one reading per device for each child.
y <- cbind(reference,new)
n <- nrow(y); k <- ncol(y); grand <- mean(y)
ms_subject <- k*sum((rowMeans(y)-grand)^2)/(n-1)
ms_device <- n*sum((colMeans(y)-grand)^2)/(k-1)
residual <- sweep(sweep(y,1,rowMeans(y)),2,colMeans(y))+grand
ms_error <- sum(residual^2)/((n-1)*(k-1))
icc_a <- (ms_subject-ms_error)/(ms_subject+(k-1)*ms_error+k*(ms_device-ms_error)/n)
icc_c <- (ms_subject-ms_error)/(ms_subject+(k-1)*ms_error)
stopifnot(abs(icc_a-.9854217)<1e-6,abs(icc_c-.9971900)<1e-6,icc_a<icc_c)
print(c(ICC_absolute_single=icc_a,ICC_consistency_single=icc_c))

learningObjectives: Distinguish association, agreement and reliability.

keyConcepts.explanation: Mean difference ± 1.96 SD estimates an interval containing about 95% of individual differences when the differences are approximately normal and their spread is stable. Confidence intervals around the limits quantify uncertainty in their estimates.

Look for proportional bias, changing spread and unusual pairs. Repeated measurements per person need analyses that account for their dependence. A clinically acceptable difference should be decided independently of the observed limits.

Compare observed agreement with agreement expected from the marginal category frequencies under independent classification. Kappa changes with category mix even at similar observed agreement. Show counts, agreement and uncertainty.

Quantifies the proportion of variability attributable to differences among subjects under a specified model. Use consistency for ranking and absolute agreement when the values must match. Name one-way or two-way model, fixed or random raters as appropriate, single or average measurement and confidence interval. A broad subject range can produce a high ICC despite important differences in units.

misconceptions.claim: A high correlation means interchangeable devices.
misconceptions.correction: A shift in every value can leave correlation unchanged. Compare paired differences with a clinical tolerance.

misconceptions.claim: The limits are a 95% confidence interval for bias.
misconceptions.correction: That interval concerns uncertainty in the mean difference. The limits describe the spread of individual differences.

misconceptions.claim: A high ICC removes the need to check absolute differences.
misconceptions.correction: Inspect the measurement-unit differences and context. ICC depends on how heterogeneous the subjects are.

The upper agreement limit still exceeds the example tolerance. In the categorical example, 88 of 100 ratings agree and unweighted kappa is approximately 0.75.

title: Audit and monitoring improvement over time
topic: Clinical standards, control charts and case mix
objective: Choose a measure and chart for the service question, then respond appropriately to observed variation.
summary: An audit defines a standard, eligibility and a denominator, checks current care, acts on findings and remeasures. Quality improvement measures are followed in time order with a stable definition. A control chart estimates expected variation in a stable process. A p-chart models the proportion of eligible encounters with a binary outcome and its limits vary with denominator. Clinical targets, control limits and confidence intervals serve different purposes.
challenge: Two emergency department months each have 15% delayed reviews. One month has 100 eligible encounters and the other has 300. Could their statistical signals differ?
steps: In this fictional emergency department audit, the adverse outcome is a first clinical review recorded more than 60 minutes after arrival among eligible encounters with known review times. Review exclusions and quantify missing timestamps before comparing months. Enter the 14 chronological counts and eligible totals or run the supplied R script. Use only months 1–12 as the illustrative baseline and hold its 8% centre fixed. Under the simple binomial model the 3 SD upper limit is about 16.1% at n=100 and 12.7% at n=300. Both later months are at 15%, but only the larger month breaches its limit. Plot a separate 5% example service target. StatsDirect Graphics → Control illustrates fixed bands for a continuous series; use this R exercise for changing binomial limits.

# Fictional ED audit. A patient encounter contributes at most one delayed review.
month <- 1:14
eligible <- c(100,125,150,100,175,125,100,150,125,175,100,175,100,300)
delayed <- c(7,11,11,10,12,9,9,13,10,14,7,15,15,45)
baseline <- 1:12
p0 <- sum(delayed[baseline])/sum(eligible[baseline])
observed <- delayed/eligible
band <- 3*sqrt(p0*(1-p0)/eligible)
lcl <- pmax(0,p0-band); ucl <- pmin(1,p0+band)
signal <- observed>ucl | observed<lcl
stopifnot(abs(p0-.08)<1e-12,all(abs(observed[13:14]-.15)<1e-12),
          identical(which(signal),14L),ucl[13]>.15,ucl[14]<.15)
print(data.frame(month,eligible,delayed,observed,lcl,ucl,signal))
plot(month,observed,type="o",ylim=c(0,max(ucl,observed)),pch=19,
     xlab="Month",ylab="Delayed review proportion",main="Fictional ED p-chart")
abline(h=p0,lty=2)
abline(h=.05,lty=3)
lines(month,lcl,lty=4); lines(month,ucl,lty=4)
abline(v=12.5,lty=2,col="grey50")
points(month[signal],observed[signal],pch=19,col="red")
legend("bottomleft",c("Baseline centre","Service target","Control limits"),lty=2:4,bty="n")

# Separate example: episodes during person-time, by frailty stratum.
# Rows are sites and columns are low/high frailty. All rates per 1,000 days.
cases <- rbind(A=c(1,18),B=c(8,8))
days <- rbind(A=c(1000,3000),B=c(4000,1000))
crude <- 1000*rowSums(cases)/rowSums(days)
standard <- drop(1000*(cases/days)%*%c(.5,.5))
stopifnot(all.equal(unname(crude),c(4.75,3.2)),
          all.equal(unname(standard),c(3.5,5)),crude[1]>crude[2],standard[1]<standard[2])
print(cbind(crude,standardised=standard))

learningObjectives: Define a reproducible process measure, denominator and audit standard.

keyConcepts.explanation: Predefine eligibility, outcome, target and data source. Report missingness, compare performance with the standard, investigate causes, act and repeat. Monitor balancing measures such as review quality or staff burden.
With stable risk p and independent observations, limits are p ± 3√[p(1−p)/n], bounded by 0 and 1. Small counts, clustering or extra variability can require another method.

Check an unusual point against data quality, eligibility and local process changes before acting. Stable but inadequate performance calls for process redesign; repeatedly reacting to ordinary fluctuations can worsen variation. Annotate and revise the centre after evidence of a sustained change.

Control limits describe expected variation of subgroup proportions under a stable baseline. Confidence intervals quantify uncertainty in an estimated parameter. The service target expresses the desired performance.

Compare strata and apply common standardisation weights when useful. An adjusted rate depends on the target mix and measured variables. Different ascertainment, missingness or sparse counts still matter. A stable chart does not prove that adjustment is adequate.

misconceptions.claim: A point beyond the control limit proves an intervention worked.
misconceptions.correction: It is a reason to investigate. Data definition, case mix, staffing and chance remain possible explanations.

misconceptions.claim: All monthly percentages have the same precision.
misconceptions.correction: With different denominators their expected variability can differ markedly.

misconceptions.claim: A point within its control limits meets the performance standard.
misconceptions.correction: The target can lie well below a stable but inadequate process.

misconceptions.claim: A 95% confidence interval can replace a 3 SD control line.
misconceptions.correction: The interval and control line answer different questions.
